client_context: A 31-year-old new mother who has been drinking wine nightly since the baby was born to cope with postpartum stress. Partner is supportive but worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — grab whatever seat works. You mentioned you're between classes, so no pressure to get cozy or anything. I'm just glad you made it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, thanks. Sorry, I'm like — I have class in 45 minutes so I might have to bolt kind of fast. But I'm here. I showed up, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: 45 minutes is plenty. So — what's going on? What made you reach out?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. So. Okay. I've been drinking. Like wine, every night, since the baby came. And something happened last week that kind of... I don't know. I can't stop thinking about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about that — the thing you can't stop thinking about.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: So I went to pick my daughter up from the crib — she was crying — and I realized I was kind of... foggy? Like not drunk-drunk but I wasn't sharp. And I just stood there for a second and thought... this isn't right. She's three months old and I'm not fully there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You noticed something felt off. Like your body was there but you weren't fully present.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yeah. And she needs me to be... I mean she's a baby, she can't do anything herself. And that scared me. Like, actually scared me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fact that it scared you — that says something real about the kind of mom you're trying to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm trying. I'm so tired. Like everyone says that but I genuinely don't think I've slept more than four hours in a row since November. My brain is just... it's always going.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Since November — so basically right from the start. When did the wine thing begin?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like the first week home from the hospital. My partner would get her down and I'd just... pour a glass. And then it was two glasses. And now on a bad night it's... I don't know, close to a bottle probably.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it started as one glass and kind of quietly crept up from there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah but I'm not — like I'm not drinking during the day. I'm never drunk around her. I always wait until she's down, mostly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's the wine doing for you? Like when you pour that first glass, what actually happens?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The noise in my head stops. That's the only way I can describe it. Like all the anxiety, all the 'am I doing this right', 'is she breathing', 'did I ruin her by doing that thing wrong' — it just... quiets.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's the only off switch you've found.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. My partner tries to help but he goes back to work, he sleeps through the night, and I'm the one up at 2am and 4am and... the wine is like my thing. My reward for surviving the day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does he think about how much you're drinking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He's worried. He hasn't said it directly but I can tell. He'll go 'another glass?' and I just... I get defensive. Which I know. I know that's a thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can already read the concern on him, even without him spelling it out.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I get it, I would be worried too. I just... I don't have another way right now. Like what am I supposed to do instead? That's the actual question.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really important question and I want to come back to it. But first — when you imagined coming here today, what did you hope would happen?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I just needed to say it out loud to someone who wouldn't... freak out. My mom would lose her mind. My friends would judge me. I just needed somewhere I could say it and not have it become a whole thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took guts. Seriously. A lot of people with exactly what you're describing never walk through a door like this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I almost didn't. I sat in my car for like ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What made you get out of the car?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That moment. The foggy moment. I keep coming back to it. Like... what if she really needed me — like an emergency — and I wasn't sharp enough. What if that happens and I'm... not right.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She's the reason you got out of the car.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, she is. And I thought I'd feel embarrassed saying all of this but I just feel... sad. Like I'm sad that this is where I ended up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does 'where you ended up' look like from the inside? If you had to describe it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Stuck. Like I'm doing everything I can just to survive but I'm also... slowly making it worse. The wine helps me get through the night but then I wake up feeling gross and anxious and then I need it again the next night. It's a loop.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm tracking this right. You're exhausted, you're kind of isolated — partner's back at work, you can't really talk to your mom or friends — and the wine became the one thing that gives you relief at the end of a brutal day. But you're starting to see that it's not actually solving anything. It's more like... borrowing against tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Borrowing against tomorrow. Yeah. That's exactly what it is. I've never heard it put that way but yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So given all that — what do you think actually needs to shift?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I need to find something else. Some other off switch. Because I can't just white-knuckle it — I've tried that. The anxiety just builds and builds and then I can't sleep at all and the next day is even worse.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I share something with you? What you're describing — the anxiety that won't quit, the not sleeping, the feeling like you're barely keeping your head above water — that's really consistent with postpartum anxiety. Which is incredibly common, and very treatable. The wine isn't a character flaw. It's you trying to self-medicate something that actually has real clinical options.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Wait, postpartum anxiety is like... a separate thing? I thought it was just postpartum depression. I didn't know anxiety was its own thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, PPA might actually be more common than PPD — it just gets talked about way less. And here's the thing: if we can address what's underneath, the wine might just stop feeling necessary.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That would be... I mean, that would be huge. Because I don't actually want to be drinking this much. I really don't. I don't even like who I am right now when I think about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't want this. The drinking isn't who you are — it's what you've been doing to survive.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And like — I do have moments where I'm a good mom. Where everything clicks and she laughs and I think, okay, I've got this. I just need more of those. I want more of those.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay, you've got about fifteen minutes. What feels like the most important first step to you — not to me, to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Probably talking to my OB. About the anxiety specifically. I've been skipping my follow-up appointments. I just kept putting it off because I didn't want to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really solid first step. And honestly? That's a call you could make before you even walk into class today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I have their number in my phone. I've been looking at it for like two weeks. I kept not pressing call because I was scared they'd think I was falling apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were scared of what they'd think. But you just walked in here and told me everything in under 40 minutes. I'd argue that's not someone falling apart — that's someone putting herself back together.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay stop, don't make me cry, I have class in like twelve minutes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay, okay — rapid fire, no crying. You showed up. You named what's going on. You connected it to your daughter. You've got a concrete next step. That is not nothing. Can we find a time in the next week or two to keep going?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I want that. Thank you. Like... genuinely. I feel like I can actually breathe a little.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again, Harold. You came back — that means something. A lot of people don't make it to a second session.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... I said I'd come back, so. I'm a man of my word, at least.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate that. So tell me — how's the week been since we last talked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ah, same as always. Long. Too quiet. I sat in that damn house for three days straight before I went out to get groceries. That was my big outing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three days alone in the house. That sounds exhausting in a different kind of way — not physically, but... something heavier.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't know how to describe it. It's like... you wake up and there's nothing. Nobody needs anything from you. You're just — there. Taking up space.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was retirement supposed to look like for you? When you imagined it back when you were still working?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I figured I'd travel a bit, maybe golf. My wife and I had plans — but she passed, that was four years ago now. And then COVID came and that kind of... I don't know, it just never got going, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You lost your wife, then the pandemic took away any chance to rebuild a routine. That's a lot of losses stacking up on each other.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to sit here and — look, I'm not looking for sympathy. It is what it is. Life doesn't go how you plan it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough — you're not here for sympathy. So let me ask you directly: how much have you been drinking this past week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I had a few drinks most nights. Maybe... maybe more than a few. Look, it's not like I'm drinking in the morning or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Evenings mostly. And when you say more than a few — what does that actually look like on a typical night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Three, four. Sometimes five if I can't sleep. I pour a glass, watch TV — it passes the time. I'm not hurting anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your doctor flagged your liver numbers at the last checkup. What did you make of that when he told you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He's being — look, doctors flag everything. Every time I go in there's something. My cholesterol, my blood pressure, now this. I'm 65, not 25. Things aren't going to be perfect.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a long list of things they're watching, and this liver thing just feels like one more item on it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And I came in here because he made me, basically. I mean... I chose to come, I know that. But I don't think I have some big problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me reflect back what I'm hearing so far. You're retired, you lost your wife, your plans for retirement never got off the ground, and most days are empty and quiet. Evenings you drink — four, five drinks — partly to pass the time, partly to sleep. Your doctor has flagged your liver. And you're here, though a part of you isn't convinced there's a real problem. Does that capture it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean — when you lay it out like that it sounds... I don't know. More than it is, maybe. But yeah. Basically.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does drinking give you that nothing else does right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It doesn't — I don't need it to give me anything. I enjoy a drink. I worked for forty years. I think I've earned a drink at the end of the day without having to justify it to anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Forty years of work. You've absolutely earned the right to relax. I'm not arguing with that. I'm just curious — what does it feel like, that first drink? What shifts?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It feels like... something loosens up. The quiet isn't as loud, if that makes any sense. I don't know — it's stupid.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The quiet isn't as loud — that's not stupid at all, actually. That's a really vivid way to put it. What is it about the quiet that gets to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because it's — you know what, I don't want to do this. Sit here and talk about how lonely I am like some kind of... I had a life. A career. A wife. Kids who don't call enough. I'm not some sad case.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not a sad case. You're a man who had a full life and is trying to figure out what it looks like now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I miss having somewhere to be. Something that needed me there. Even if work was a pain in the ass, at least someone needed me to show up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You miss being needed. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. It's not. And the drinking — honestly? I know it's not great. I'm not dumb. I can feel it's gotten heavier. But what am I supposed to do instead, just sit there sober in the quiet?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said you can feel it's gotten heavier. What have you noticed — what does that look like day to day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I wake up and my stomach's off. I get foggy. Forget things. Last Tuesday I couldn't even remember if I'd locked the door. Kept getting up and checking. Three times.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's starting to spill into your days in ways that are hard to ignore.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And the liver thing — I laughed it off but... I don't want to end up in a hospital bed. Alone. That's — that's actually a real fear of mine, if I'm being honest.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real honesty to say that — especially when you walked in today not entirely sure you even had a problem.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I still don't know if I'd call it a problem, exactly. But... I don't know. Something has to change. I can't keep doing this and just pretend everything's fine. That's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something has to change — you said that yourself. If you picture six months from now and things are actually different, what would you want that to look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd want to... sleep better. Not feel like garbage every morning. Maybe actually call my daughter instead of just thinking about it for three weeks and not doing it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Better sleep, feeling better physically, more connection with your daughter. Those things clearly matter to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's in Denver. We talk maybe once a month. It's not her fault — I don't reach out either. I think I'm embarrassed about how I've been living, honestly. I don't want her to know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That self-awareness — recognizing the embarrassment, naming it — that matters. What would need to be different for you to feel okay picking up the phone and calling her?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd have to feel like I'm... doing something. Like I'm not just sitting around drinking every night. I couldn't tell her that's my life right now. I don't want that to be my life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what you've shared today. You came in thinking this maybe wasn't a real problem — but as we've talked, you've acknowledged the drinking has gotten heavier, it's affecting your sleep, your memory, how your mornings feel. Your liver is being watched. You're lonely and you miss being needed. And underneath all of it — you don't want this to be your life. You want to reconnect with your daughter, and to be someone you feel okay being. That's a lot of honesty for one session.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... pretty much right. I didn't expect to say half of that when I walked in here today.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's why you came back. Even when part of you didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess so. I think... I think I'm more ready to actually do something than I thought I was when I got here. I don't know what yet. But sitting still isn't working.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So as a starting point — not a big overhaul, just one small step — what's something you'd be willing to try before we meet next?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I could try... not having that first drink until after nine. Or just — call my daughter. Something small. I think I can do something small.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for being here. I know doing this over video can feel a little strange the first time. Before we get into anything, I just want to check in — how are you feeling right now, just being here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... honestly? A little weird. Like, I don't really do therapy. My old therapist — she's the one who kind of pushed me toward this, so... yeah. I don't really know what I'm supposed to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes something — just showing up when it feels unfamiliar. I appreciate you being here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... I figured I'd at least try, you know? See what happens.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What is it that your therapist noticed that made her think this might be a good idea for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She, uh... she knew about the drinking. Like, I'd mentioned it a couple times. She said she thought it was worth talking to someone who specifically deals with that kind of stuff.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So drinking came up enough in your conversations with her that she wanted you to have a space dedicated to it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, yeah. I don't think it's like... a huge deal or anything. I'm a bartender. It's kind of just part of the job, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about what that looks like — drinking as part of the job.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: So I work like, four nights a week usually. Sometimes five. And after a shift, especially a long one, you just... you need to decompress. It's loud, it's hectic, people are in your face all night. Most of the staff, we'll just have a couple drinks after close. It's like... it's just how you wind down.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's almost like a ritual. The shift ends and there's this built-in way to let the pressure out.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Yeah. It's not like I'm sitting there getting wasted every night. It's just... it's part of how the night ends.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And outside of work — on your days off, what does drinking look like then?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I still drink on my days off. Like, it's not tied to work really. I'll have some beers watching a game or whatever. Or if I'm hanging out with people. Or even just... by myself, I guess. Just to relax.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's become something that shows up pretty much every day, whether you're working or not.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean, when you say it like that... yeah. I guess it is every day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's it like to hear yourself say that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Weird. Like... I don't know. I hadn't really thought about it that way. I've just been doing it, you know? It's not like I wake up and think 'oh I gotta drink today.' It just... happens. But yeah. I think... I actually can't remember the last time I didn't. Like, a full day where I just didn't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That landed somewhere for you. The not being able to remember.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It's like... that's the thing that's been sitting in the back of my head, I think. That was the thing I told my old therapist. And saying it out loud right now it just feels kind of... heavy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: ... I'm just going to sit with that with you for a second.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... [long pause] ...I don't know. It scared me a little when I realized it. Like, that's not normal, right? I know plenty of people who drink, but they also just... don't sometimes. And I just... don't do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does 'normal' look like to you, when you imagine it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Just being able to take it or leave it? Like my buddy Jake — he'll have a beer at a barbecue and then just stop. Doesn't think about it. And I'm always kind of watching that and thinking like... how does he just stop? Like that seems almost impossible to me now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's something about watching Jake that makes you wonder about yourself. Like his ease with stopping is a mirror somehow.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's a good way to put it. Because I used to be like that. In college I drank but it wasn't every single day. I'd have whole weekends where I just didn't bother. And somewhere along the way that just... stopped happening.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When do you think that shift happened?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Probably when I started bartending full-time. Three years ago maybe. It kind of crept up. I never made a decision to drink every day. It's just... the culture, the hours, the late nights. It was all just so gradual.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're doing something right now that takes real honesty — looking back and actually tracing how you got here, not just where you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess I'm good at not looking at stuff. Like I can go a long time without examining things. But this one... I don't know, it's been harder to ignore lately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's made it harder to ignore lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... I had this shift last month where I was just off. Like physically off. My hands were a little shaky in the morning. And I thought — okay, that's dehydration, right? But then I had a drink and I felt better and I was like... oh. That's not dehydration.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You felt the drink fix something that shouldn't have needed fixing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I didn't let myself think about it for like two weeks. I just buried it. But it kept coming back up. That's probably why I actually followed through on coming here today.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took courage — following through even when part of you wanted to stay buried.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know about courage. It's more like I got tired of feeling like something was just... wrong, in the background. You know what I mean? Like a low hum of something being off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A low hum. Something you can't quite turn off.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And it's like... I'm 27. I'm not trying to be that guy. The bartender who's just pickled by forty. I've seen those guys at work — the lifers — and they just look tired in a specific way. And I don't want that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's a version of yourself in the future you're already moving away from. What does the version you want to move toward look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I haven't thought that far. I guess just... being able to sleep without needing something first. Waking up and not already calculating the day around when I'll have a drink. That sounds so simple but it feels really far away right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sleep that's just sleep. Days that aren't organized around drinking. That matters to you deeply.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It's like... I miss feeling like I was just living. Not like I was managing something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think that version of you — the one who's just living — needs most right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Probably to stop pretending this is fine. Like, I came in here saying it's not a big deal. But I think... I think I've known for a while that it kind of is. I just didn't want to say it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You named it. Right here, right now — you said the thing you've been carrying quietly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [quiet laugh] I did, didn't I. It feels... I don't know. Weird. But also kind of like... okay. Like maybe it's okay to say it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I've heard today, if that's alright. You came in a little uncertain, not sure therapy was really for you. But as we talked, you shared something important — that drinking has become a daily constant, something that shows up even when you don't plan for it. You noticed something one morning with your hands that you couldn't quite explain away. You've watched people around you who just stop, and it feels foreign now. There's a younger version of you who didn't live this way, and a future version you don't want to become. And today, you said out loud — maybe for the first time — that you think this actually is a big deal. That's a lot to hold.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [pause] That is a lot. I didn't expect to feel like this after just... talking. I thought I'd come in, answer some questions, and leave. But it's more than that, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It usually is. As we close out today — what feels most important to take with you from this conversation?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think just... that I said it. That I actually admitted it's more than just unwinding after work. I don't know what I'm going to do about it yet, but I needed to hear myself say it. So... I think I want to come back. If that's okay.

client_context: A 26-year-old software engineer with severe social anxiety who uses alcohol as liquid courage at every social event. Knows it's a crutch but terrified of life without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm glad you made it. Before we get into anything, I just want you to know this is a pretty low-pressure space — nothing you say here leaves this room. So, what brings you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... honestly? My sister kind of made me come. She's been on my case about it for a few months and I just figured it was easier to show up than keep having the same argument over and over.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's she been worried about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My drinking, mostly. She thinks I drink too much when we go out. Which... I mean, it's not like I'm sitting at home drinking alone every night or anything. It's always social.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the way you see it, this is social drinking — it happens when other people are around, not something you're doing by yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. I'm not like... I don't have a problem problem, you know? It's just parties and work events and stuff. That's pretty normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does drinking actually do for you in those situations?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It... um. It just makes it easier. Like, I have really bad anxiety around people — especially people I don't know well — and a couple drinks kind of turns the volume down on all of that. I can actually hold a conversation without feeling like I'm going to crawl out of my skin.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Alcohol gives you access to a social life that feels almost impossible without it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: 'Impossible' is... I don't know, that might be a strong word. But yeah, kind of. Without it my brain just won't shut up. Every little thing feels like a test I'm failing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me what's actually happening in your head when you're at a party sober.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... it's a lot. Like, I'm constantly scanning everything. Did I say something weird? Is this person bored? Do they want me to leave? Am I laughing at the right things? It's like running a hundred background processes at once. I can't just... be there. I'm always one step removed, watching myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds genuinely exhausting — carrying all of that monitoring while also trying to seem relaxed and connected.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It really is. Most people have no idea that's what's going on when I seem totally fine on the outside. I've gotten really good at faking it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: How much are you usually drinking at these events?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Depends on the event. Like, a house party with friends maybe four or five drinks. Work things are worse — probably six or seven because I'm even more anxious around coworkers. There's more at stake, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Work events actually feel more dangerous than regular social ones — higher stakes, more anxiety, more drinks to manage it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... yeah. I mean, I know six or seven sounds like a lot, but I can hold my liquor pretty well. My tolerance is high. I'm usually functional.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does the day after one of these events look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Usually pretty rough. Headache, sometimes I can't totally piece together how the night ended. I've canceled plans because I was too hungover to leave my apartment. It kind of wipes out the whole next day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So pieces of the night go missing, and then the whole next day is gone too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it that way... yeah. That's kind of a lot of time, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does that lost time cost you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My coding, honestly. I do my best work on weekends and if Saturday morning is a write-off, I've kind of blown it. And I've missed brunch with my mom twice in the last month. She didn't say anything but... I could tell she was hurt. That one actually bothers me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm getting this right. You've got really real, painful anxiety that makes social situations feel almost unsurvivable on your own. Drinking has been how you get through that — your way in the door. But it's starting to cost you things that actually matter. Your work. Your mom. Parts of nights you can't get back. Does that track?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. I haven't actually said all of that out loud before. It sounds different when you say it back.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's it like to hear it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Weird. Kind of uncomfortable. I think I've been... really deliberate about not letting myself look at it too directly. Like if I don't fully look, it's not fully real.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Keeping busy enough that the full picture never quite comes into focus.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's exactly it. I'm actually really good at that. Software engineers are great at staying busy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If drinking wasn't part of the equation at all — what do you imagine social situations would actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Terrifying. I genuinely don't know if I could do it. I've been drinking at every party since I was like nineteen. I don't even know what sober-me at a social event looks like. I've never really... tested it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really honest answer. You're not pretending this would be simple — you're looking at it straight.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I mean... part of me actually wants to know. Like, can I connect with people without it? Can I be interesting without it? I genuinely have no idea and that's... that's kind of scary but also kind of interesting?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a curious part of you underneath the fear — something that wants to find out who you actually are in those moments.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I think I'd like to be someone who could just... show up. Without all the prep. I just don't know where you even start with something like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Would it be okay if I shared some of what we know about how alcohol and anxiety actually interact? Just the research side of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, definitely.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So here's the thing that tends to surprise people — alcohol doesn't actually treat anxiety. In the moment it feels like relief, and that feeling is real. But what it's actually doing is training your brain to need it in order to cope, and over time it lowers your baseline threshold for anxiety. So the sober version of you at a party gets more anxious the longer this goes on, not less. You're not building tolerance to the social situations — you're building dependence on the substance. The good news is that social anxiety is one of the most treatable things we work with. CBT, exposure work — people come out the other side of this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Wait — so it's actually making my anxiety worse? Like it's not just not helping, it's actively making it harder? That's... huh. That actually makes a disturbing amount of sense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's a bit of a trap — the thing that feels like the solution is quietly feeding the problem.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My anxiety has gotten worse over the past few years, not better. I just assumed that was... adulthood. More responsibilities, more people to impress. But maybe it's not just that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If things could actually change — what would you want to be different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to go to my work holiday party and not need three drinks before I even walk in the door. I want to have a real conversation with someone and actually remember all of it the next morning. I want to stop dreading every single social thing that gets added to my calendar.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those are really specific, concrete things — not vague wishes. That tells me a lot about what actually matters to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I've wanted those things for a while. I just... never let myself believe they were actually possible for someone like me. Like maybe that was just for people whose brains worked normally.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So — you came in today because your sister pushed you to. And somewhere in the last hour, you started talking about what you actually want. Less anxiety running the background. Better memory. Real connections. A work event you can walk into without a drink in your hand. You see the cost clearly, and you can also see what a different version of this could look like. That's a lot of ground to cover in a first session.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is a lot. I feel kind of... lighter? Which is weird because nothing is actually fixed. I thought this would feel worse than it does.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What feels like a next step that could actually fit your life right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... actually talking to someone about the anxiety itself. Like treating that directly instead of just managing it with drinks. And coming back here. I think I want to keep doing this. Which is not what I expected to say when I walked in.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for coming in. I know you mentioned you were between things — I'll keep an eye on the time with you. What brings you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I saw the flyer and honestly I don't even know why I'm here. I'm not, like, some alcoholic or whatever. I just drink sometimes. Everyone does.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you isn't even sure this is the right place to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. I work twelve-hour shifts in the ER. I watch people die. I come home and I have a couple glasses of wine to wind down. That's not — that's just coping. That's what everybody does.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does winding down look like for you on a typical night after a shift?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I pour a glass as soon as I get through the door. Sometimes two. Or three. Whatever. It's literally the only thing that shuts my brain off. I've tried other stuff — running, meditating for like two weeks — nothing works.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The only thing that shuts it off.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I don't have time to be doing yoga at eleven at night when I get off at ten. I have to be back at six AM. So what am I supposed to do, just lie there staring at the ceiling?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've actually tried other things. A lot of people don't even get that far.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. None of it stuck. And I still had to be functional the next morning so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's it like when you get home after one of the really bad ones?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's like... I can't even explain it. My brain won't stop. I'll be making dinner and I'm still in that room where the guy died. Like I'm physically still there. And the wine just... it takes the edge off. That's all it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're still in that room even when you're standing in your own kitchen.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And people don't get that. My boyfriend is like, 'just go to sleep.' I can't just go to sleep. I've got all this — I don't know. Stuff. In my head.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What kind of stuff?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Images. Sounds. The codes that go bad. The kids — the kids are the worst. You just... you carry all of that home with you and nobody sees it. Nobody wants to see it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You carry all of it and nobody sees it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. So no, I don't think I need to be here. I think I need a different job, maybe. Or a week off. But I don't have either of those options so I don't know what you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say you're doing fine — what does that actually look like these days?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I show up. I do my job. Sometimes I'm a little tired but everyone in the ER is tired. That's just the job, that's not a me thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A little tired.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay, more than a little sometimes. Fine. I had to call out once last month. But I was actually sick. That wasn't — that wasn't because of the drinking.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't have to tell me that. That took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't even know why I said it. [pause] It was one time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If your coworkers knew you were sitting here right now — what do you think they'd think?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They'd probably say I don't need to be here. Half the nurses I know drink. It's like this unspoken occupational thing. Nobody talks about it but everybody does it. I'm not some outlier.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The culture kind of normalizes it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. So why am I the one sitting here? I genuinely don't get it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's actually a real question. Why are you here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe because... I got scared. A little. I woke up one morning and I couldn't remember the end of the night. Like I remembered pouring the third glass and then I was just in bed. And that hadn't — that hadn't happened before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That scared you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. A little. I mean — I'm not blacking out every night or anything. That was once. But I kept thinking about it. I couldn't stop thinking about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was going through your mind as you kept coming back to it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I thought... I know what this looks like. I see it in patients. I know the progression. I just never — I don't know. I never thought I'd be the one looking at it from the inside.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've been using alcohol to get through genuinely brutal shifts — and in some ways it's been working. Your brain gets a break. But lately something shifted. You called out. There was that night you can't fully account for. And some part of you picked up a flyer and walked in here today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. When you lay it out like that it sounds... [trails off] yeah. I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If a patient walked into your ER and described exactly what you've just described to me — what would the nurse version of you think?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh that's — [pause] that's not fair. [quiet laugh] She'd be concerned. She'd probably say get some help. Like, that's a pattern. That's literally what I'd say to someone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She'd be concerned.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. God. I hate that. [pause] I know exactly what I'd say. I'd say, 'this is going to escalate if you don't address it.' I say that to patients all the time. I just didn't think I'd be saying it about myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've got a lot of insight. Being able to hold both the nurse perspective and your own experience at the same time — that's genuinely not easy to do.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... knowing it and actually stopping it are two completely different things. I know what alcohol does physiologically. I know the science. Doesn't stop me from pouring the glass when I get home.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If you could change just one thing about how you're managing the stress right now — just one — what would it be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd want something else that actually works. Not yoga, not an app. Something real. Because I don't want to end up being the nurse who makes a mistake because she's half-asleep and still half-drunk from the night before. I don't want to be that person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't want to be that person. Protecting your patients — that matters to you, a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's the one thing I'm most scared of, honestly. I care about my patients. I'm good at my job. That's — that's the thing I can't screw up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would actually taking care of yourself look like — the way you'd want one of your patients to take care of themselves?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Probably... actually talking to someone. Not a hotline, like a real person, regularly. And maybe setting some kind of limit on the drinking. Not stopping cold — I don't think I'm there yet — but like, not three glasses on a Tuesday just to function.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you walked in here not totally sure why, a little skeptical, and now you're talking about seeing someone regularly, setting some limits, protecting your career and your patients. You arrived with a lot of reasons why this wasn't necessary, and somewhere in here you found your own reasons why maybe it is. That's worth paying attention to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I still think I'm probably fine. But... maybe I should actually make an appointment. A real one. [pause] I'll think about it.
